This is the pattern of a systematic error, such as a scale that is out of calibration; it can be fixed by recalibrating. B: accurate means close to the true value; 72.4 kg is not close to 70.1 kg. C: the readings are precise, but precision alone does not make them correct. D: the readings are within 0.1 kg of each other, so they are precise.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{11}\)
question: In lab, a student correctly records a volume as "5.0 mL." Later, on a practice medication order, the student writes "5.0 mg" and ".5 mg." Explain why the lab entry is correct but both order entries should be rewritten.
answer: In a lab notebook, the trailing zero in 5.0 mL tells the reader the volume was measured to the tenths place, which is good significant-figure practice. On medication orders, The Joint Commission's "Do Not Use" list forbids trailing zeros ("5.0 mg" can be misread as 50 mg if the decimal point is missed) and requires a leading zero (".5 mg" can be misread as 5 mg). The order should read 5 mg and 0.5 mg . Lab reports and medication orders follow different rules because they guard against different risks: hiding precision in one, a tenfold dosing error in the other.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{12}\)
question: A lab reports serum potassium as 4.1 mmol/L. How many significant figures does it have, and what does the report claim about the uncertainty? Why would the lab not report 4.137 mmol/L, even if the analyzer displayed it?
answer: 2 significant figures ; the value is reliable to the tenths place (uncertain by about ±0.1 mmol/L). Reporting 4.137 would claim precision to the thousandths place that the method cannot deliver, which would make small, meaningless changes from day to day look like real changes in the patient.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{13}\)
question: Calculate and round correctly: (a) 12.45 mL + 3.1 mL + 0.567 mL; (b) 4.50 cm × 0.0320 cm; (c) 98.6 °F − 97.92 °F; (d) 2.0 g ÷ 3.000 mL.
answer: (a) 16.117 → 16.1 mL (addition: fewest decimal places, tenths from 3.1). (b) 0.144 → 0.144 cm 2 (multiplication: fewest significant figures, 3; the units multiply too). (c) 0.68 → 0.7 °F (subtraction: tenths, from 98.6). (d) 0.6667 → 0.67 g/mL (division: 2 significant figures, from 2.0).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{14}\)
question: Round 6,451.7 to 2 significant figures. A. 6.5 × 10 3 B. 650 C. 6.4 × 10 3 D. 6,450
answer: A. Underline the second digit (6, 4 51.7); the digit to its right is 5, so round the 4 up to 5. Then keep the number's size with placeholder zeros or scientific notation: 6,500 or 6.5 × 10 3 . B: drops a placeholder zero; 650 is ten times too small. If someone owed you $6,500 and paid $650, you would notice. C: cuts off (truncates) instead of rounding; the 5 after the underlined digit means round up. D: keeps 3 significant figures, not 2.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{15}\)
question: Calculate (25.62 − 3.4) × 1.205 ÷ 2.50 to the correct number of significant figures.
answer: Work the parentheses first: 25.62 − 3.4 = 22.22. The subtraction is good to the tenths place, so underline the last significant digit: 22. 2 2 (3 significant figures). Keep all the digits and continue: 22.22 × 1.205 ÷ 2.50 = 10.71. The fewest significant figures in the multiplication and division steps is 3 (22.2 and 2.50), so the answer is 10.7 . Round only at the end.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{16}\)
question: A pressure ulcer measures 2.5 cm by 1.25 cm. Estimate its area (length × width) with the correct units and significant figures.
answer: 2.5 cm × 1.25 cm = 3.125 cm 2 → 3.1 cm 2 (2 significant figures, from 2.5 cm). Multiplying cm by cm gives cm 2 .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{17}\)
question: (a) A glass thermometer is marked every 1 °C. The liquid ends about four-tenths of the way from 37 to 38. Record the reading. (b) A graduated cylinder is marked every 1 mL. The bottom of the meniscus sits about three-tenths of the way from 23 to 24. Record the volume.
answer: Estimate one digit past the smallest marking. (a) 37.4 °C (3 significant figures; the 4 is estimated). (b) 23.3 mL , read at the bottom of the meniscus. Writing 37 °C or 23 mL would throw away information you measured.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{18}\)
question: A digital analytical balance displays 2.0500 g. What should you record? A. 2.0500 g B. 2.05 g C. 2.050 g D. 2 g
answer: A. Record every digit a digital balance shows, including trailing zeros; they are measured, so 2.0500 g has 5 significant figures. B: drops two measured zeros and makes the balance look 100 times less precise than it is. C: drops one measured zero. D: throws away almost all of the measurement.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{19}\)
question: A newborn weighs 7.25 lb. What is the weight in kilograms? (1 kg = 2.2046 lb)
answer: \( 7.25\ \text{lb} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{kg}}{2.2046\ \text{lb}} = 3.289\ \text{kg} \to \) 3.29 kg (3 significant figures). Size check: the number of kilograms is less than half the number of pounds.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{20}\)
question: (Math practice only.) An order is written as 0.250 mg. How many micrograms (mcg) is this? A. 2.50 × 10 2 mcg B. 2.50 × 10 −4 mcg C. 25.0 mcg D. 2.50 × 10 5 mcg
answer: A. \( 0.250\ \text{mg} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{g}}{1000\ \text{mg}} \times \dfrac{10^{6}\ \text{mcg}}{1\ \text{g}} = 250.\ \text{mcg} = 2.50 \times 10^{2}\ \text{mcg} \). A smaller unit gives a bigger number. B: divides by 1000 instead of multiplying; the factor 1000 mcg = 1 mg was used upside down, and the number got smaller even though the unit got smaller. C: uses 100 mcg = 1 mg, a made-up factor. Go through the base unit and use factors from the sheet. D: multiplies by 10 6 as if the order were in grams; it skips the mg → g step and is 1000 times too large.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{21}\)
question: A cup of yogurt is labeled 6.0 oz. What is its mass in grams? (1 g = 0.03527 oz)
answer: \( 6.0\ \text{oz} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{g}}{0.03527\ \text{oz}} = 170.1\ \text{g} \to \) 1.7 × 10 2 g (2 significant figures, from 6.0 oz; "170 g" also shows 2 under this book's rule).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{22}\)
question: Convert 4.5 × 10 −3 kg to milligrams.
answer: \( 4.5 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{kg} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{kg}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{g}} = \) 4.5 × 10 3 mg (through the base unit, grams).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{23}\)
question: A resting heart rate is 72 beats/min. About how many times does the heart beat in one day?
answer: \( \dfrac{72\ \text{beats}}{1\ \text{min}} \times \dfrac{60\ \text{min}}{1\ \text{h}} \times \dfrac{24\ \text{h}}{1\ \text{day}} = 103{,}680 \to \) 1.0 × 10 5 beats/day (2 significant figures, from 72; the time factors are exact).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{24}\)
question: A blood glucose result is 110 mg/dL. Express it in g/L. (10 dL = 1 L)
answer: \( \dfrac{110\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{dL}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{g}}{1000\ \text{mg}} \times \dfrac{10\ \text{dL}}{1\ \text{L}} = \) 1.1 g/L (110 has 2 significant figures under this book's rule).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{25}\)
question: The speed limit on a stretch of Highway 99 is 65 mi/h. What is this in m/s? (1 mi = 1.6093 km)
answer: \( \dfrac{65\ \text{mi}}{1\ \text{h}} \times \dfrac{1.6093\ \text{km}}{1\ \text{mi}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{h}}{60\ \text{min}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{min}}{60\ \text{s}} = 29.06 \to \) 29 m/s (2 significant figures). Distance first, then time.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{26}\)
question: (Math practice only.) An IV runs continuously at 125 mL/h. How many liters does it deliver per day? A. 3.00 L/day B. 3.00 × 10 3 L/day C. 5.21 × 10 −3 L/day D. 0.125 L/day
answer: A. \( \dfrac{125\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{h}} \times \dfrac{24\ \text{h}}{1\ \text{day}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{L}}{1000\ \text{mL}} = 3.00\ \text{L/day} \) (3 significant figures; 24 h = 1 day is exact). B: 3000 is the number of milliliters per day; the mL → L step was skipped. C: divides by 24 instead of multiplying; "per hour" on the bottom needs 24 h on the top of the next factor to cancel. D: converts mL to L but never converts hours to days, so it is still the volume per hour.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{27}\)
question: Convert 4.0 × 10 4 cm 2 to m 2 . A. 4.0 m 2 B. 4.0 × 10 2 m 2 C. 4.0 × 10 8 m 2 D. 0.040 m 2
answer: A. \( 4.0 \times 10^{4}\ \text{cm}^{2} \times \left(\dfrac{1\ \text{m}}{100\ \text{cm}}\right)^{2} = 4.0 \times 10^{4} \div 10^{4} = 4.0\ \text{m}^{2} \). B: divides by 100, forgetting to square the factor. C: multiplies by 10 4 ; the factor is upside down, and a bigger unit must give a smaller number. D: divides by 10 6 , cubing a factor that should be squared (this is an area, not a volume).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{28}\)
question: A patient room is 12.0 ft long, 10.0 ft wide, and 8.00 ft high. What is its volume in m 3 ? (1 ft = 30.48 cm, exact)
answer: V = 12.0 × 10.0 × 8.00 = 960. ft 3 . \( 960.\ \text{ft}^{3} \times \left(\dfrac{30.48\ \text{cm}}{1\ \text{ft}}\right)^{3} \times \left(\dfrac{1\ \text{m}}{100\ \text{cm}}\right)^{3} = 27.18\ \text{m}^{3} \to \) 27.2 m 3 (3 significant figures).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{29}\)
question: A bag of IV fluid holds 0.75 L. Express its volume in cm 3 and in cc.
answer: \( 0.75\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{cm}^{3}}{1\ \text{L}} = \) 7.5 × 10 2 cm 3 = 7.5 × 10 2 cc (750 mL; 1 mL = 1 cm 3 = 1 cc). In charting, write mL.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{30}\)
question: (Math practice only; not dosing guidance.) A child weighs 55.0 lb. A medication is ordered at 10. mg per kg of body weight per dose. The oral liquid contains 100. mg per 5 mL (5 mL is a defined label volume). What volume is one dose? (1 kg = 2.2046 lb)
answer: \( 55.0\ \text{lb body} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{kg body}}{2.2046\ \text{lb body}} \times \dfrac{10.\ \text{mg drug}}{1\ \text{kg body}} \times \dfrac{5\ \text{mL}}{100.\ \text{mg drug}} = 12.47\ \text{mL} \to \) 12 mL (2 significant figures, from 10. mg/kg). Check: 55 lb is about 25 kg; 25 × 10 = 250 mg; 250 mg is 2.5 times 100 mg, so 2.5 × 5 mL = 12.5 mL.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{31}\)
question: A manufacturer has 2.0 kg of a drug. How many 500. mg tablets can it make?
answer: \( 2.0\ \text{kg} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{kg}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{tablet}}{500.\ \text{mg}} = \) 4.0 × 10 3 tablets (2 significant figures, from 2.0 kg).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{32}\)
question: A nursing student drives from Fresno to a clinical site in Merced, 65 mi away, on a foggy morning at an average of 45 mi/h. How many minutes does the drive take? A. 87 min B. 1.4 min C. 42 min D. 2.9 × 10 3 min
answer: A. Start with the term that stands alone (65 mi): \( 65\ \text{mi} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{h}}{45\ \text{mi}} \times \dfrac{60\ \text{min}}{1\ \text{h}} = 86.7 \to 87\ \text{min} \) (2 significant figures). The city names and the fog are distractors. B: 1.4 is the time in hours ; the h → min step was skipped. C: uses the speed upside down (45 mi/h × 60 ÷ 65); miles do not cancel. D: multiplies 65 mi by 45 mi/h, which gives mi 2 /h, not a time.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{33}\)
question: Normal saline is 0.90% NaCl, meaning 0.90 g of NaCl per 100 mL of solution. How many grams of NaCl are in a 1.000 L bag?
answer: \( 1.000\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{0.90\ \text{g NaCl}}{100\ \text{mL}} = \) 9.0 g NaCl (2 significant figures, from 0.90%).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{34}\)
question: A patient's hematocrit is 42%, meaning red blood cells make up 42% of the blood volume. If the patient has 5.0 L of blood, what volume is red blood cells?
answer: \( 5.0\ \text{L blood} \times \dfrac{42\ \text{L RBC}}{100\ \text{L blood}} = \) 2.1 L of red blood cells (2 significant figures). Check: a part is always smaller than the total.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{35}\)
question: A cough syrup has a density of 1.31 g/mL. What is the mass of 60.0 mL of it?
answer: \( 60.0\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{1.31\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mL}} = \) 78.6 g (3 significant figures). A syrup is denser than water, so 60 mL weighs more than 60 g.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{36}\)
question: What volume of glycerol (d = 1.26 g/mL) has a mass of 75.6 g? A. 60.0 mL B. 95.3 mL C. 0.0600 mL D. 0.0167 mL
answer: A. \( 75.6\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mL}}{1.26\ \text{g}} = 60.0\ \text{mL} \) (3 significant figures). A liquid denser than water has fewer mL than g. B: multiplies by the density (75.6 × 1.26); grams do not cancel, and the volume came out larger than the mass, which is impossible for a liquid denser than water. C: 0.0600 is the volume in liters , labeled as mL. D: divides the density by the mass (1.26 ÷ 75.6); the units would be 1/mL, not mL.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{37}\)
question: A patient produces 1.50 L of urine in a day, with a specific gravity of 1.015 (so a density of 1.015 g/mL). What is its mass in kilograms?
answer: \( 1.50\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{L}} \times \dfrac{1.015\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mL}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{kg}}{1000\ \text{g}} = 1.5225\ \text{kg} \to \) 1.52 kg (3 significant figures, from 1.50 L).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{38}\)
question: After a delivery, soaked pads weigh 410. g; the same pads dry weigh 96 g. (a) Estimate the blood loss in mL with the rule 1 g ≈ 1 mL. (b) Recalculate using a blood density of 1.06 g/mL. (c) Which estimate is larger, and why?
answer: Blood mass = 410. g − 96 g = 314 g (both masses are known to the ones place, so the difference is too). (a) 314 mL . (b) \( 314\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mL}}{1.06\ \text{g}} = 296.2 \to \) 296 mL . (c) The 1 g ≈ 1 mL rule gives the larger estimate, because blood is slightly denser than water, so each gram of blood is a little less than 1 mL. The difference (about 6%) is small enough that the quick rule is used in practice. (Context only.)

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Label each observation qualitative or quantitative: (a) the urine sample is dark amber; (b) the patient weighs 72.5 kg; (c) the reaction mixture fizzed; (d) the oxygen flow is 2 L/min.
answer: (a) qualitative (a color, no number); (b) quantitative (number and unit); (c) qualitative; (d) quantitative.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: A farmer tests whether a new drip-irrigation schedule increases almond yield. One block of trees keeps the old schedule; a matching block gets the new one. At harvest, she weighs the almonds from each block. Name the independent variable, dependent variable, and control.
answer: Independent variable: the irrigation schedule (the one thing she changed). Dependent variable: the mass of almonds harvested (what she measured). Control: the block kept on the old schedule.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Which statement is a scientific law, and which is a theory? (a) Matter is made of atoms that are rearranged, not created or destroyed, in chemical reactions. (b) In a chemical reaction, the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
answer: (a) is a theory: it explains why, using a model of atoms. (b) is a law: it states what always happens (the law of conservation of mass).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Write in scientific notation: (a) 93,000,000 mi; (b) 0.000482 g; (c) 0.07050 L.
answer: (a) 9.3 × 10 7 mi (the trailing zeros are placeholders). (b) 4.82 × 10 −4 g. (c) 7.050 × 10 −2 L (the final zero is significant, so it stays).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Write in standard form: (a) 7.04 × 10 −3 m; (b) 3.1 × 10 5 platelets/µL.
answer: (a) 0.00704 m (negative exponent: move three places left). (b) 310,000 platelets/µL (positive exponent: move five places right).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A student writes 0.0056 as 5.6 × 10 3 . Without redoing the problem, how can a calculator show that this is wrong, and what is the correct answer?
answer: Typing 5.6 × 10 3 into the calculator gives 5600, not 0.0056, so the sign of the exponent is wrong. The decimal point moves three places to the right, so the answer is 5.6 × 10 −3 .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: Calculate, and give the answer in scientific notation: (a) (4.0 × 10 8 )(2.5 × 10 −3 ); (b) (9.0 × 10 4 ) ÷ (3.0 × 10 −2 ).
answer: (a) 4.0 × 2.5 = 10, and 8 + (−3) = 5, so 10 × 10 5 = 1.0 × 10 6 (2 significant figures). (b) 9.0 ÷ 3.0 = 3.0, and 4 − (−2) = 6, so 3.0 × 10 6 .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
question: (Context only.) One lab reports a white blood cell count as 6.4 × 10 3 /µL, and another reports a count for a different patient as 6.4 × 10 9 /L. Which patient has more white blood cells per unit of blood?
answer: Neither: they are the same. 6.4 × 10 9 per liter, divided by 10 6 microliters per liter, is 6.4 × 10 3 per microliter. The exponents differ only because the units differ.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Give the symbol and the power of ten for each prefix: (a) mega-; (b) centi-; (c) micro-; (d) pico-.
answer: (a) M, 10 6 . (b) c, 10 −2 . (c) µ (mcg for micrograms in health care), 10 −6 . (d) p, 10 −12 .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: The yellow sheet lists milli- as 10 −3 and nano- as 10 −9 , so 1 mm = 10 −3 m and 1 ng = 10 −9 g. Rewrite each equality in whole-number form.
answer: 1000 mm = 1 m (because 1 ÷ 10 −3 = 1000), and 10 9 ng = 1 g (because 1 ÷ 10 −9 = 10 9 ).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Which is larger: (a) 0.50 mg or 450 mcg; (b) 1.2 dL or 120 mL?
answer: (a) 0.50 mg = 500 mcg, so 0.50 mg is larger. (b) 1 dL = 0.1 L = 100 mL, so 1.2 dL = 120 mL: they are equal .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: (Context only.) A child's weight is entered as "20" in a chart field labeled kg, but the child was weighed on a scale reading pounds. Is a weight-based dose calculated from this entry too large or too small, and by about how much?
answer: Too large. 20 lb is only about 9 kg (20 ÷ 2.2046 = 9.07), so treating it as 20 kg makes the calculated dose about 2.2 times too large. This is why many facilities record weights in kilograms only.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
question: Which of these US–metric equalities are exact: 1 in = 2.54 cm; 1 kg = 2.2046 lb; 1 L = 1000 cm 3 ; 1 gal = 3.785 L?
answer: 1 in = 2.54 cm and 1 L = 1000 cm 3 are exact (definitions). 1 kg = 2.2046 lb (5 significant figures) and 1 gal = 3.785 L (4 significant figures) are rounded values.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A note in a patient's chart reads "Temp 37.2, weight 64." What is missing, and why does it matter?
answer: Both units are missing. 37.2 is a normal body temperature in degrees Celsius but would be impossible in degrees Fahrenheit, and 64 could be kilograms or pounds, a difference of about 2.2 times. Without units the reader has to guess, and a guess about weight can change a weight-based dose.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Identify the number and the unit: (a) 250 mL; (b) 4.1 mmol/L of potassium; (c) one dozen syringes.
answer: (a) 250, milliliters. (b) 4.1, millimoles per liter (a combined unit). (c) 1, dozen syringes (a counted unit; one dozen is exactly 12).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: How many significant figures are in each? (a) 0.0400 g; (b) 60.50 mL; (c) 7,000 m; (d) 7,000. m; (e) 3.010 × 10 4 cells; (f) 0.008 L.
answer: (a) 3 (leading zeros do not count; the trailing zeros after a decimal point do). (b) 4. (c) 1 (no decimal point). (d) 4 (the decimal point makes the trailing zeros count). (e) 4 (every digit in A). (f) 1.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Write 45,000 g so that it shows (a) 2, (b) 3, and (c) 5 significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Which of these have an unlimited number of significant figures? (a) 60 s = 1 min; (b) a blood pressure of 118 mmHg; (c) 4 vials on a tray; (d) 1 kg = 2.2046 lb.
answer: (a) and (c). The first is a definition and the second is a count. A blood pressure is measured (3 significant figures), and 2.2046 lb is a rounded value (5 significant figures).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A newborn scale is tested with a 5.000 kg reference mass. It reads 5.120 kg, 5.118 kg, and 5.121 kg. Is the scale accurate, precise, both, or neither? Which target in Figure 1 does it match?
answer: Precise but not accurate: the readings agree within 0.003 kg, but all are about 0.12 kg (120 g) too high. This matches target (a). The scale needs to be recalibrated.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
question: (Context only.) Rewrite each medication amount the way a safe order would write it, and explain the change: (a) .25 mg; (b) 10.0 mg.
answer: (a) 0.25 mg : a leading zero is required, so the decimal point cannot be missed (".25" could be read as "25"). (b) 10 mg : no trailing zero, so the order cannot be misread as 100 mg. In a lab notebook, by contrast, 10.0 mg would be correct if the mass was measured to the tenth of a milligram.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Round each to the number of significant figures shown: (a) 76,349 (2); (b) 0.0049872 (3); (c) 6.0449 × 10 −3 (2).
answer: (a) 76,000 (the next digit is 3, so round down; the zeros hold the place). (b) 0.00499 (the next digit is 7, so round up: 498 becomes 499). (c) 6.0 × 10 −3 (the next digit is 4, so round down; the zero stays as the second significant figure).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Calculate and report with the correct significant figures and units: (a) 0.0457 cm × 2.1 cm; (b) 45.82 mL + 3.6 mL − 0.555 mL.
answer: (a) 0.09597 cm 2 → 0.096 cm 2 (2.1 has 2 significant figures). (b) 48.865 mL → 48.9 mL (3.6 has one decimal place).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Calculate (8.47 g − 6.2 g) × 4.105, where 4.105 is a measured value with no unit. Show the underline step.
answer: Parentheses first: 8.47 − 6.2 = 2.27 g; one decimal place, so underline 2. 2 7 (2 significant figures). Then 2.27 × 4.105 = 9.318 g. The answer gets 2 significant figures: 9.3 g .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A bottle of 40 tablets (counted) has a total tablet mass of 15.2 g. What is the average mass of one tablet?
answer: 15.2 g ÷ 40 = 0.38 g. The 40 is exact, so 15.2 g (3 significant figures) decides: 0.380 g . The trailing zero must be written to show 3 significant figures.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
question: A student adds 132 mg of a salt to 2.50 g of water and reports the total as 134.50 g. Find two mistakes and give the correct total in grams.
answer: The student added milligrams to grams directly, and reported too many decimal places. Convert first: 132 mg = 0.132 g. Then 2.50 g + 0.132 g = 2.632 g → 2.63 g (two decimal places, from 2.50).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{6}\)
question: Three measurements of a patient's forearm length are 24.6 cm, 24.9 cm, and 24.7 cm. What is the average length?
answer: (24.6 + 24.9 + 24.7) ÷ 3 = 74.2 ÷ 3 = 24.733… cm. The sum has one decimal place (74. 2 , 3 significant figures), and 3 is exact: 24.7 cm .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A buret is marked every 0.1 mL. The bottom of the meniscus is between the 18.3 mL and 18.4 mL marks, about seven-tenths of the way down to 18.4. Record the reading.
answer: 18.37 mL (18.3 is certain; the 7 in the hundredths place is estimated). Readings of 18.36 or 18.38 mL are also reasonable.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: An analytical balance displays 5.200 g. A student records "5.2 g." What is wrong, and how many significant figures should the recorded mass have?
answer: The balance measured the two trailing zeros, so they are significant. The student threw away two digits of precision. Record 5.200 g , which has 4 significant figures .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A 100 mL graduated cylinder is marked every 1 mL. Which reading could have come from it: 36 mL, 36.4 mL, or 36.42 mL? Explain.
answer: 36.4 mL. With 1 mL marks you are certain of the ones place and estimate the tenths. 36 mL leaves out the estimated digit; 36.42 mL claims a second estimated digit that the marks cannot support.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A bathroom scale shows 68 kg; a clinic scale shows 68.4 kg for the same person a minute later. Which reading tells you more, and why?
answer: The clinic reading, 68.4 kg. It has three significant figures and is known to the nearest tenth of a kilogram; 68 kg is known only to the nearest kilogram. (Whether either scale is accurate is a separate question; see Section 1.3.1.)

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Write two conversion factors for each equality: (a) 1 L = 1000 mL; (b) 1 kg = 2.2046 lb. Which factors are exact?
answer: (a) \( \tfrac{1000\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{L}} \) and \( \tfrac{1\ \text{L}}{1000\ \text{mL}} \), exact (a metric prefix). (b) \( \tfrac{2.2046\ \text{lb}}{1\ \text{kg}} \) and \( \tfrac{1\ \text{kg}}{2.2046\ \text{lb}} \), measured (5 significant figures, the yellow sheet's value).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: A patient is 68.5 in tall. What is the height in centimeters?
answer: \( 68.5\ \text{in} \times \dfrac{2.54\ \text{cm}}{1\ \text{in}} = 173.99\ \text{cm} \to \) 174 cm (3 significant figures from 68.5 in; 2.54 is exact).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A 2.00 L bottle of an oral rehydration drink holds how many quarts? (1 qt = 0.946 L)
answer: \( 2.00\ \text{L} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{qt}}{0.946\ \text{L}} = 2.114\ \text{qt} \to \) 2.11 qt (3 significant figures from 2.00 L and from 0.946).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A student converts 12.5 oz to grams using the yellow sheet's 1 g = 0.03527 oz and writes 12.5 oz × (0.03527 oz / 1 g) = 0.441. What went wrong, and what is the correct answer?
answer: The factor is upside down: ounces are on top twice, so they cannot cancel, and the answer's unit would be oz 2 /g. Correct: \( 12.5\ \text{oz} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{g}}{0.03527\ \text{oz}} = 354.4\ \text{g} \to \) 354 g . Size check: a gram is much smaller than an ounce, so the number must get bigger.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Convert 11.84 µs to milliseconds.
answer: \( 11.84\ \mu\text{s} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{s}}{10^{6}\ \mu\text{s}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{ms}}{1\ \text{s}} = \) 1.184 × 10 −2 ms (0.01184 ms; 4 significant figures).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Convert 3.549 lb to milligrams. (1 lb = 453.59 g)
answer: \( 3.549\ \text{lb} \times \dfrac{453.59\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{lb}} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{g}} = 1{,}609{,}791\ \text{mg} \to \) 1.610 × 10 6 mg . The measurement has 4 significant figures and the factor 453.59 has 5, so the answer has 4; scientific notation shows the significant final zero.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A hemoglobin result is 13.5 g/dL. Labs in many other countries report it in g/L. Convert it.
answer: \( \dfrac{13.5\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{dL}} \times \dfrac{10\ \text{dL}}{1\ \text{L}} = \) 135 g/L (3 significant figures; only the bottom unit changes).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A simple syrup has a sugar concentration of 0.5 g/mL. Express it in kg/dL. (1 dL = 100 mL)
answer: \( \dfrac{0.5\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mL}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{kg}}{1000\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{100\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{dL}} = \) 0.05 kg/dL (1 significant figure). Answers of 50 kg/dL (forgot g → kg: 0.5 × 100) or 5 × 10 −6 kg/dL (put 100 mL on the bottom: 0.5 ÷ 1000 ÷ 100) come from one flipped or missing factor.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{5}\)
question: (Math practice only.) An IV pump is set to 125 mL/h. What is this rate in mL/min?
answer: \( \dfrac{125\ \text{mL}}{1\ \text{h}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{h}}{60\ \text{min}} = 2.083\ \text{mL/min} \to \) 2.08 mL/min (3 significant figures; 60 min = 1 h is exact).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A patient's body surface area is 1.85 m 2 . Express it in cm 2 .
answer: \( 1.85\ \text{m}^{2} \times \left(\dfrac{100\ \text{cm}}{1\ \text{m}}\right)^{2} = 1.85 \times 10^{4}\ \text{cm}^{2} \) ( 18,500 cm 2 ; 3 significant figures).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Convert 2.5 × 10 5 cm 3 to m 3 .
answer: \( 2.5 \times 10^{5}\ \text{cm}^{3} \times \left(\dfrac{1\ \text{m}}{100\ \text{cm}}\right)^{3} = 2.5 \times 10^{5} \div 10^{6} = \) 0.25 m 3 . Dividing by 100 instead (2.5 × 10 3 m 3 ) means the factor was not cubed.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A medicine cup holds 5.0 mL. Express this volume in (a) cc, (b) cm 3 , (c) L.
answer: (a) 5.0 cc and (b) 5.0 cm 3 , since 1 mL = 1 cm 3 = 1 cc. (c) \( 5.0\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{L}}{1000\ \text{mL}} = \) 5.0 × 10 −3 L .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: Explain in one or two sentences why 1 cm 2 = 100 mm 2 , using a drawing in words.
answer: A square 1 cm on each side is also 10 mm on each side, and its area is 10 mm × 10 mm = 100 mm 2 . A grid of 10 rows of 10 tiny 1 mm squares fills it.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A baker in Visalia makes 2 dozen cookies every 18 min. How many minutes does she need to make 150. cookies? (1 dozen = 12, exact)
answer: \( 150.\ \text{cookies} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{dozen}}{12\ \text{cookies}} \times \dfrac{18\ \text{min}}{2\ \text{dozen}} = 112.5\ \text{min} \) → 1.1 × 10 2 min (18 min has 2 significant figures; the city name is a distractor).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: (Math practice only.) An order calls for 0.150 g of a drug. The liquid on hand contains 250. mg per 5.00 mL. What volume holds the ordered amount?
answer: \( 0.150\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{mg}}{1\ \text{g}} \times \dfrac{5.00\ \text{mL}}{250.\ \text{mg}} = 3.00\ \text{mL} \)

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A problem says, "A 12.0 oz can of soda contains 34.0 mg of caffeine." Write the conversion factor both ways up, and say which one you would use to find the caffeine in 3 cans (36.0 oz).
answer: 34.0 mg caffeine / 12.0 oz soda, or 12.0 oz soda / 34.0 mg caffeine. To go from ounces to milligrams, ounces must be on the bottom: 36.0 oz × (34.0 mg / 12.0 oz) = 102 mg caffeine .

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: A copper ore is 0.25% copper by mass. What mass of ore, in kilograms, contains 1.00 kg of copper?
answer: \( 1.00\ \text{kg Cu} \times \dfrac{100\ \text{kg ore}}{0.25\ \text{kg Cu}} = 400\ \text{kg ore} \) → 4.0 × 10 2 kg ore (0.25% has 2 significant figures).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A 12.0 g piece of sterling silver (92.5% silver by mass) is in a ring. What mass of silver does it contain, and what mass is other metals?
answer: 12.0 g × (92.5 g Ag / 100 g sterling) = 11.1 g silver ; the other metals are 12.0 g − 11.1 g = 0.9 g (one decimal place in the subtraction).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Classify each: (a) sucrose (table sugar), C 12 H 22 O 11 ; (b) sugar dissolved in iced tea; (c) chlorine gas, Cl 2 ; (d) a bowl of cereal with milk.
answer: (a) compound (three elements bonded in a fixed ratio); (b) homogeneous mixture (dissolved evenly; strength can vary); (c) element (one kind of atom; a diatomic element); (d) heterogeneous mixture (you can see the parts).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Box (f) in Figure \(\PageIndex{1}\) contains H 2 O molecules and O 2 molecules. Explain why it is a mixture even though every particle contains oxygen.
answer: There are two different kinds of particles (H 2 O and O 2 ), and they are not bonded to each other. A pure substance would need every particle to be identical.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Which method would you use to separate (a) sand from water, (b) the dissolved salt from seawater, and (c) red blood cells from plasma?
answer: (a) filtration (or decanting); (b) evaporation (or distillation, which also recovers the water); (c) centrifugation.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A particle diagram shows a box of eight identical particles. Each particle is one formula unit made of one Na, one Cl, and one O (sodium hypochlorite, NaClO, the active ingredient in bleach). A second box shows eight identical particles, each made of two bonded Cl atoms. Classify each box.
answer: First box: one kind of particle, made of three different elements bonded, so a pure substance, a compound . Having three elements does not make it a mixture; they are bonded in one particle. Second box: one kind of particle containing only Cl atoms, so a pure substance, an element (Cl 2 , one of the diatomic seven).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A 250 mL sample of a substance is moved from a 500 mL flask to a 1000 mL flask and now fills the whole 1000 mL flask. What state is it in? Explain with the particle view.
answer: Gas. Its volume changed to fill the new container, which only a gas does; its particles are far apart and move freely until they hit the walls.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Glass holds its shape like a solid, but its particles are not arranged in a repeating pattern. What kind of solid is glass?
answer: An amorphous solid (its particles are disordered, unlike a crystalline solid).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A student spills 75.0 mL of water from a beaker onto a lab bench. It spreads into a thin puddle. Has its shape changed? Has its volume changed? Explain with the particle view.
answer: The shape changed (from the beaker's shape to the puddle's), but the volume did not: it is still 75.0 mL. Liquid particles touch one another, so they cannot be pushed closer or spread farther apart, but they slide past each other, so the liquid takes the shape of whatever holds it.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Will a fluoride ion, F − , attract or repel (a) a potassium ion, K + ; (b) a chloride ion, Cl − ?
answer: (a) attract (opposite signs); (b) repel (both negative).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: A + charge and a − charge are moved from 2 nm apart to 1 nm apart. Does the attraction get stronger or weaker? Was energy released or absorbed as they moved closer?
answer: Stronger, because they are closer. Energy was released, because opposite charges came together.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: At the same distance, which pair attracts more strongly: K + with Cl − , or Ca 2+ with O 2− ?
answer: Ca 2+ with O 2− : at the same distance, larger charges give a stronger attraction.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: Classify each as a physical or chemical change: (a) a frozen IV bag thaws; (b) milk sours; (c) a nail rusts; (d) dry ice shrinks as it sits on a lab bench.
answer: (a) physical (melting); (b) chemical (bacteria turn sugars into lactic acid, a new substance); (c) chemical (iron forms iron oxide); (d) physical (sublimation of CO 2 ).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Which of these properties of copper are intensive: mass, color, melting point, volume, density?
answer: Color, melting point, and density are intensive. Mass and volume are extensive.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: Frost forms on a windshield overnight with no liquid water ever appearing. Name this change of state and say whether it is physical or chemical.
answer: Deposition (gas to solid). It is a physical change: the water molecules are unchanged.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: What is the mass of 25.0 mL of glycerol (d = 1.26 g/mL)?
answer: \( 25.0\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{1.26\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mL}} = \) 31.5 g (3 significant figures).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: What volume of ethanol (d = 0.789 g/mL) has a mass of 150. g? A. 190. mL B. 118 mL C. 0.190 mL D. 5.26 × 10 −3 mL
answer: A. \( 150.\ \text{g} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mL}}{0.789\ \text{g}} = 190.1\ \text{mL} \to 190.\ \text{mL} \) (3 significant figures; the decimal point shows the zero is significant). B: multiplies the mass by the density (g × g/mL), so grams do not cancel; a liquid less dense than water must have more mL than g. C: is the right number of liters (0.190 L) but labeled mL. D: divides the density by the mass (0.789 ÷ 150); the units would be 1/mL, not mL, so the setup cannot be right.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A urine sample of 250. mL has a specific gravity of 1.020. Taking water's density as 1.000 g/mL, what is the mass of the sample?
answer: Density = 1.020 × 1.000 g/mL = 1.020 g/mL. \( 250.\ \text{mL} \times \dfrac{1.020\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mL}} = \) 255 g (3 significant figures, from 250. mL).

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: You need 1.50 kg of glycerol (d = 1.26 g/mL) and have only a 500-mL graduated cylinder. What volume do you need, and how would you measure it?
answer: \( 1.50\ \text{kg} \times \dfrac{1000\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{kg}} \times \dfrac{1\ \text{mL}}{1.26\ \text{g}} = 1190.5\ \text{mL} \to \) 1.19 × 10 3 mL . Fill the 500-mL cylinder twice (1000 mL), then measure about 190 mL more.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{1}\)
question: A metal cube has a mass of 54.0 g and a volume of 20.0 cm 3 . Calculate its density and use the table to identify the metal.
answer: d = 54.0 g ÷ 20.0 cm 3 = 2.70 g/cm 3 , which matches aluminum.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{2}\)
question: Vegetable oil (about 0.92 g/mL) and corn syrup (about 1.37 g/mL) are poured into a cylinder of water, and none of the three liquids mix. What is the order of layers from top to bottom? Where would a piece of cork (about 0.24 g/mL) end up?
answer: Least dense on top: vegetable oil, then water, then corn syrup on the bottom. The cork is less dense than all three, so it floats on top of the oil.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{3}\)
question: A 500. g block and a 5.00 g chip are cut from the same piece of oak. Which has the greater density?
answer: Neither: both are oak, and density is intensive, so it does not depend on the size of the sample.

title: Exercise \(\PageIndex{4}\)
question: A piece of reddish metal has a mass of 35.8 g. It raises the water in a graduated cylinder from 30.0 mL to 34.0 mL. Calculate its density and identify the metal from the table. What answer would a student get by dividing by 34.0 mL?
answer: V = 34.0 mL − 30.0 mL = 4.0 mL (one decimal place, so 2 significant figures). d = 35.8 g ÷ 4.0 mL = 8.95 g/mL → 9.0 g/mL , closest to copper (8.96 g/mL). Dividing by 34.0 mL gives 1.05 g/mL, which would mean the metal barely sinks, a sign the wrong volume was used.
